slides.title: Acid–base state and pH
bullets: The acid–base state is the relation between hydrogen and hydroxyl ions in biological media; whether a medium is acidic or alkaline depends on the H⁺ concentration: when it rises the medium is acidic, when it falls alkaline.
In practice pH is used — the negative decimal logarithm of the hydrogen-ion concentration; when H⁺ rises pH falls, and when H⁺ falls pH rises.
Blood pH is very stable: normally about 7.35–7.45.

Any shift of pH disturbs cell activity, especially enzyme systems, the binding and release of oxygen by haemoglobin, water–electrolyte and other metabolism, membrane permeability and neuromuscular excitability.

slides.title: Acid–base state and pH
bullets: Acids are constantly produced from food and metabolism (carbonic, lactic, pyruvic, acetoacetic, β-hydroxybutyric and others), yet thanks to complex regulatory mechanisms pH does not shift to the acid side.
The stability of pH is maintained by the lungs (remove CO₂), kidneys (secrete H⁺ and NH₃), liver (binds acid radicals, accumulates HCO₃⁻), the gastrointestinal tract and buffer systems.

slides.title: Buffer systems
bullets: A buffer system binds an excess of H⁺ or releases these ions; it consists of a mixture of a weak acid and its salt with a strong base.
The body’s buffer systems: haemoglobin, bicarbonate, protein and phosphate buffers.

Bicarbonate buffer: when acid increases, H⁺ combines with HCO₃⁻ to form carbonic acid, which breaks down into H₂O and CO₂, and the excess CO₂ leaves through the lungs; when alkali increases, it combines with the weak carbonic acid. When carbonic acid and bicarbonate are in a 1:20 ratio, blood pH is normal.

slides.title: Buffer systems
bullets: Haemoglobin buffer: CO₂ formed in tissues is turned into H₂CO₃ by carbonic anhydrase; HCO₃⁻ leaves the erythrocyte for the plasma (K⁺ cannot pass) and Cl⁻ takes its place; in the lungs the process runs in reverse.
The protein buffer binds H⁺ in acid medium and releases it in alkaline medium; the phosphate buffer (NaH₂PO₄ / Na₂HPO₄) is the main buffer of cells.
Buffers prevent a shift quickly but cannot hold the state for long, so the lungs, kidneys, liver and gastrointestinal tract must join in.

slides.title: Acid–base indices and the link with water–electrolyte balance
bullets: In practice these are used: actual pH, pCO₂ (respiratory component), BB (buffer base — the sum of buffer anions of blood), BE (base excess), SB (standard bicarbonate), AB (actual bicarbonate) and TCO₂ (total CO₂).

BE is the deviation of buffer bases from normal and the main indicator of the metabolic component: normally ±2.5 mmol/L; a negative value means fewer bases or more acids, a positive value the opposite.
SB is bicarbonate under standard conditions (37 °C, pCO₂ 40 mmHg, blood fully saturated with oxygen); AB is the actual bicarbonate content of the patient’s blood.

slides.title: Acid–base indices and the link with water–electrolyte balance
bullets: Knowing pH and pCO₂, the Siggaard-Andersen nomogram gives BB, BE, SB, AB, TCO₂, the form of the disturbance and the degree of compensation.

Law of electroneutrality: in any fluid medium the number of anions equals the number of cations; HCO₃⁻ is the most variable anion — when it falls (acidosis) Cl⁻ and residual anions rise, when it rises (alkalosis) Cl⁻ falls.

Law of isoosmolarity: the osmolarity of plasma, interstitial and intracellular fluid is the same (normally 285 mOsm/L); when the acid–base state is disturbed the electrolyte and water balance changes too, and vice versa.

slides.title: Methods of determining sodium, potassium, chloride. Clinical and diagnostic significance?
bullets: 1. Sodium is the main extracellular cation (normal ~136–145 mmol/L), determines osmolality and volume; potassium is the main intracellular cation (~3.5–5.0 mmol/L), membrane potential, heart rhythm; chloride is the main anion, acid-base balance.

2. Method – ion-selective electrodes (ISE): direct (undiluted – blood gas analyzers) and indirect (diluted – large biochemistry analyzers); with indirect ISE, hyperlipidemia and hyperproteinemia give false hyponatremia.

slides.title: Methods of determining sodium, potassium, chloride. Clinical and diagnostic significance?
bullets: 3. Potassium preanalytics: hemolysis, fist clenching, prolonged tourniquet, K-EDTA contamination, thrombocytosis/leukocytosis (in serum) give false hyperkalemia – when in doubt remeasure in heparinized plasma; storage in the cold also raises K.
4. Hyponatremia: water excess (SIADH, heart/liver failure), Na loss (diuretics, vomiting, adrenal insufficiency); hypernatremia – water loss, diabetes insipidus.

slides.title: Methods of determining sodium, potassium, chloride. Clinical and diagnostic significance?
bullets: 5. Hyperkalemia: renal failure, hypoaldosteronism, drugs, cell breakdown, acidosis; hypokalemia: diuretics, vomiting/diarrhea, hyperaldosteronism, alkalosis.
6. Chloride: falls in metabolic alkalosis (vomiting), rises in hyperchloremic acidosis; used in interpreting the anion gap (Na − (Cl + HCO3)).

slides.title: Biological significance of water-electrolyte metabolism?
bullets: 1. Water makes up ~60% of body weight in adults: ~2/3 inside cells, ~1/3 outside cells (interstitial and intravascular).
2. Water is a solvent and transport medium, thermoregulation, the medium of metabolic reactions.

3. Electrolytes: Na⁺ – the main cation of extracellular fluid (osmolality and volume), K⁺ – intracellular (membrane potential, neuromuscular excitability), Cl⁻ and HCO3⁻ – the main anions (acid-base balance), Ca²⁺, Mg²⁺ – enzymes, contraction, hemostasis.

slides.title: Biological significance of water-electrolyte metabolism?
bullets: 4. Plasma osmolality (~275–295 mOsm/kg) is determined mainly by Na; oncotic pressure is provided by albumin.
5. Disorders: dehydration/overhydration, imbalance of sodium and potassium – neurological and cardiac complications; laboratory monitoring – electrolytes, osmolality, hematocrit, protein.

slides.title: Regulation of water-electrolyte metabolism?
bullets: 1. Osmoregulation: hypothalamic osmoreceptors sense a rise in plasma osmolality → thirst and secretion of ADH (vasopressin) → via V2 receptors in the renal collecting ducts aquaporin-2 – water reabsorption.
2. Volume regulation: the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system – aldosterone in the distal nephron increases Na reabsorption and K excretion; its secretion is regulated by K⁺ level and the RAAS.
3. Natriuretic peptides (ANP, BNP) – natriuresis and vasodilation when volume increases.
4. The kidney is the final effector organ: filtration, reabsorption, concentration.

slides.title: Regulation of water-electrolyte metabolism?
bullets: 5. Laboratory reflection: plasma and urine osmolality, Na, K, urine Na; ADH disorders – diabetes insipidus (urine dilute, hypernatremia), SIADH (hyponatremia, urine concentrated).
